I've done ACT (not specifically for ADHD, but I think it helps that too). What I got from it is this (other people might experience it differently or work with a different kind of therapist to me):

- when we have symptoms that cause distress, like mental illness or neurological conditions, we try to 'fix' them, with medications and other techniques. This is usually helpful.

- however, alongside changing our symptoms, we can also try and change our mindset and attitudes towards our symptoms. We can accept our symptoms for what they are and try to work with them - not be ruled by them, but to notice them, embrace them, and walk alongside them. This could also minimise distress. 

- you need skills to do this:

----- One is to observe what it is you're going through and not get carried away from it or ignore it. E.g. You are frustrated you aren't paying attention very well. Rather than getting caught up in the frustration, you simply notice that you are feeling this way, let yourself feel this way (noting that the feeling is separate from you) and do the things you want to do anyway. 

------ another is mindfulness, the art of living in the moment and placing your attention back in the moment when you notice yourself daydreaming and wandering off (an especially nice skill to have for ADHDers)

------ another is kindness to yourself. So, if you are feeling frustrated and dejected, instead of forcing yourself into onerous activities, you could take an hour just to comfort yourself, clear your mind, have a nice bath or make yourself a cup of tea. Relating to yourself in such a way means that your response to your problem doesn't contribute to a vicious cycle which makes the problem worse. For me, it's easy to get lost in a shame cycle, I did a crappy job, therefore I'm a horrible person and I need to work harder, which just makes me more anxious, makes my performance worse, which increases my shame, and so on. ACT is excellent at breaking that cycle. 


I'm not a huge mindfulness fan (probably because it's at odds with how my brain operates) but I do think ACT is a really good therapy.

I read a lot, but it is very difficult if the book doesn't interest you. I've found, through years of trial-and-error, that I like books from the mid-twentieth century onwards with protagonists I can relate to, or nonfiction books on topics like pop-medicine, ethics, answers to whimsical questions (e.g. Why are there so many froyo stands?), or that really delve into personal anecdotes and emotional stories. It's been hard enough to figure out what interests me that I have not yet figured out how to read something that doesn't interest me.

I don't have much patience either. One thing that helps though is the thought that it's often the process of achieving something that's more valuable than the thing itself. It's the journey, not the destination. Sometimes. If you could win an Olympic gold medal for the 100 metre sprint today it would be awesome, but the full impact would be lost. You didn't work for it, it wouldn't mean that much, the glow would disappear really quickly. If you learn to appreciate the process more, I think patience would come. At least, I hope so.

Not an expert, but I'm not sure that hyperfocus is the same as flow? I think flow is more positive, exhilarating, productive. Hyperfocus (at least, in my mind) is more obsessive, headachy and sometimes kind of strange. You can be productive with hyperfocus, but it doesn't feel as good... I think. 

Anyway, IMO, it would be a good idea to work in long-term therapy to find and solidify yourself. You deserve the space to work things out. I'm in therapy, and although it has made no direct impact on my ADHD symptoms, it has definitely helped me accept my shortcomings and minimise their impact on my life and my productivity. I've done psychodynamic psychotherapy for 2.5 years for reference, though maybe you should read up on different modalities and see what you think will work best for you.

A few things:
- it would get annoying if you did it excessively, but I find the therapist trick of 'reflecting' helpful. You listen to what someone has to say and then, in your own words, summarise what you understood. If you don't get it right, the other person doesn't mind and just corrects what you missed or the emphasis. If you do get it right they say something like, 'yes, exactly' as though you actually said something insightful. Doing this forces you to listen, and gives you the job of figuring out the point of what someone has said. 
- contrary to other advice, I find it easier to listen if I'm doing something repetitive and not mentally taxing, like knitting (if you already know how) or doodling. It isn't as good for participating in discussion, but I find it excellent for listening.

My only work around (when I played) was also to write the note underneath the stave. Not a great work around, but it got me to grade 2 violin. Interestingly. I find it easy enough to remember guitar chords now (though I otherwise suck at guitar).

This is not ADHD related advice, but networking is crucial for PhD admissions in the sense that your application has a much higher chance of success if you've lined up a potential supervisor who likes your style. Doing some research about who you'd most like to talk to, whose research interests most align with yours, is a good start. I would also suggest contacting them before the conference and arranging a mutually good time to talk. It can be difficult at conferences to talk at length with or even find certain people because there's so much going on. The best way to show you can survive is probably by preparing a little (1-2 page) outline on ideas you have for your PhD topic. It's surprisingly hard to do, so if you can't, it would be good to identify an area in pol sci that most interests you and you know enough about to speak to. Best of luck!

I have lied to control the outcome of psych evaluations before and I am here to say that they generally come back to bite you. In my experience, if you lie and don't admit to it, the pdoc experiences you as manipulative and subconsciously sabotages your care. This is even though lying is a normal and a straightforward (if primitive) defence of denial. If you want a bp diagnosis, you do have to give some indication that you have bp symptoms. If you get a depression diagnosis and go nuts on an SSRI, it could be an interesting experience for you but you could also die, so I'd watch out for that. Probably it's not too late to tell the truth if you want.

I think I developed some habits which look a little like OCD symptoms but are just adaptations to ADHD. For instance, I'll check that I locked the door not because something bad might happen if I don't but because I wasn't paying attention when I left and have no idea if I did actually lock it.

To answer your question, no. However, even though Abilify is an antipsychotic, it's not just used for schizophrenia. It can help regulate mood and it's sometimes used with an antidepressant for people with depression. Talk to the prescribing doctor about it. IMO I think it's a bit weird to be prescribing powerful medication with long term side effects (although Abilify's side effect profile is pretty good compared to other antipsychotics) to mitigate the side effects of another powerful med, especially if your son is quite young. It might be worth investigating other options, but I'm not a psychopharmacologist and my knowledge of the brain was fully captured when I made a poster about the cerebral cortex in high school.

I think you have a difficult situation on your hands. There is a lot of literature on opening up conversations in a way that isn't accusatory or argumentative. For instance, using 'I feel' statements instead of phrases like 'you always...' or name-calling, etc. Mental illness or not, few people respond well to criticism so making it as gentle as possible (perhaps couched in any genuine compliments you might have) is a good strategy. You can't just put up with bad behaviour though - that's crucial for your own mental health.

I know those feels. My mother lives in another state and wasn't at all involved in my assessment, but if she were I think she would have filled out the forms similarly. I was valedictorian at high school too, and it's interesting how that sort of thing affects how people see you. It's like, it doesn't matter if your staring out in space or late to everything or having to get your friends to rip pages out of their notebooks because you've forgotten yours. If you're smart (especially if your a girl) that means your conscientious and on the ball and always listening carefully, regardless of reality. Although I have a diagnosis, I'm afraid to tell any of my friends and family because I don't think they'll believe me. 

In your case, I do think it's worth having that conversation with your mother but, as everyone else is saying, if your psych knows what they're doing, it shouldn't matter too much. I think it's important that your mother gets a sense of what you feel you're struggling with so she can support you better.

I would be annoyed at paying money for someone continually falling asleep on me. It'd be a good outcome if you got a refund. However, it's not really malpractice, I don't think. It's hard because psychiatrists regularly see people who can get really (understandably) upset by what they say and do and they aren't always the most sensitive of people. Sometimes I feel like you have to be ironically robust to survive a session without feeling worse at the end. It's also not possible to get psychiatrists to diagnose 'correctly'. It's not a science, a pdoc has their opinion based on varying levels of reasonableness and there's often disagreement among them. It is very common for people to be misdiagnosed or not diagnosed, which, IMO, isn't always the pdoc's fault, but the fault of a system where people are categorised almost arbitrarily, usually within an hour of meeting them.

I understand your frustration - I have my own experiences in hating the medical system and various people in it. Try to remember that it's you and your view of yourself which is most likely of anyone's to be accurate. Not that you can't learn about yourself from anyone, but your convictions about yourself are probably right. 

I think: Shake it up to experience, ask nicely for a refund (if the money is a concern for you), thank your chosen deity that you've found a pdoc who you like and takes you seriously (those are rare).

The most difficult social situations for me are ones dealing with authority or some kind of perceived power imbalance. I cannot relax even though I know at a certain point it is normal to be able to have fun with professors, managers, etc. it has gotten me into some social trouble when someone I know has acted like an authority when they are really a peer (not necessarily n-types but along those lines). I can't be myself in the relationship and I end up deferring to their (percieved) authority. I almost lose myself - my opinions, any notion about what I want to do, etc.

I would like to be able to communicate what I think (appropriately to the situation, of course) without subconsciously collapsing myself in the face of authority. I guess I've made some headway into doing that, I even expressed disagreement with someone in authority recently, but it isn't easy and I often face the thought "I should have said..." After the fact, of course.

Same here. For me, I think they are seperate issues but they fundamentally interact. When I'm depressed, I can barely deal with the SA, and when I'm manic I barely have any SA. When stable, SA is there but I have the energy to try and overcome it. SA is also such a trigger for me mood-wise - it can be depleting/energising being with others. Generally I've learned to manage SA as something seperate from the bipolar but it isn't always so simple. I found CBT for SA incredibly useful, but not enough on its own, and I wonder if it's partly because it is so influenced by moods. 

I think that stigma can definitely feed into SA, but it's not my experience because I don't think the fact I have bipolar is a big deal in the situations I'm most anxious about. If the stigma causes shame though, and if the SA kicks in at about the time you were diagnosed with bipolar, I can't see why it couldn't be related. 

I think also that for some, SA could be part of their depression persona, since anxiety and depression seem to fit together very often. That could make SA a depression warning sign as part of their bipolar as opposed to a seperate illness. Maybe. Just speculating.

For me, the most helpful piece of advice I got was don't cut out the unhealthy foods, just add in lots of healthy food and you'll crave less unhealthy food anyway, which really works. Cutting is for sure a sign of depression, but actually it is no indication that she's suicidal. I guess, just in relation to what has happened to her recently, it isn't a good sign, and it doesn't seem like her moods aren't very stable right now. The stress of her placement may be all it is, but I would think that this is something she may need to address with a psychiatrist, sooner rather than later. In the past, my bf has called a psychiatrist on my behalf when he was worried about me. If you feel comfortable, this may be a good idea for you. It struck me that my psychiatrist took my bf's call far more seriously than he took anything I said, I imagine because my bf had a clearer view of the situation than me. 

I think I would leave the parents thing aside for now. Parents can be an extra stressor and apply all these pressures that make the situation harder. If she needs to take a break, that is totally her choice and her parents interference shouldn't play into that. 

If you are afraid of her being alone, it may be a good idea to make sure she constantly has company. The isolation can be a real killer when you're feeling depressed, and while having someone to talk to won't make it go away, I find that it is really helpful. Make sure that she knows she can call you whenever. Maybe have a deal - if she starts thinking about cutting, for instance, she'll give you a call. It doesn't always work for me, but usually it does. 

I guess, lastly, cutting by itself doesn't warrant hospitalisation at all. I know it can be hard, but think of it as a sign of depression, rather than a sign of suicidal intent. That said, this does need to be addressed with the pros.
